lessons.title: Event loop and promises
lessons.concept: JavaScript finishes the current synchronous call stack before running promise reactions from the microtask queue. A promise is therefore not its final value but a contract that will later be fulfilled or rejected. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. That map lets you predict where code runs and where each failure must be handled.

explanation.title: Mental model
explanation.text: JavaScript finishes the current synchronous call stack before running promise reactions from the microtask queue. A promise is therefore not its final value but a contract that will later be fulfilled or rejected. First draw the inputs, transformations, trust boundaries, and outputs. explanation.title: Simple analogy
explanation.text: promise execution order is like an order ticket handed to a kitchen that announces when the meal is ready. The analogy helps you remember the main journey, but running code is the evidence: inspect every value at the input, during transformation, and at the output.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: The call stack runs console.log A and schedules the then callback; it immediately continues to B before draining the microtask queue. Start with the smallest working version and inspect its real value in the terminal or DevTools before adding an abstraction.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: The pending, fulfilled, and rejected states are exclusive: a settled promise never changes again, which stabilizes the contract for every consumer. Then connect the rule to the contract between browser, server, and database; every boundary needs a defined input and an explicit failure.

explanation.title: Understand it deeply
explanation.text: then transforms a value and always returns a new promise; returning each link avoids nested callbacks and preserves one error path. Finally test the normal case, a boundary input, and a deliberate failure so the behavior is proven beyond the happy path.
